newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands expected at new march for jobs.
newsitem.headline: Thousands expected at new march for jobs.

text.p: Police said on Wednesday they expected up to 15,000 people to turn up for a march for work on Thursday through this central Belgian city.

The march, against the backdrop of company closures, tightening budgetary belts and stubbornly high unemployment, is one of a series that have already taken place or are planned in the run up to a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16.

Trades unions, working under the slogan of less work to create more jobs, want to force the leaders of the 15-member EU to agree rules to allow working hours to be cut in order to open the way for the creation of more employment.
They also want government to cut the tax costs of employment, introduce tax policies that encourage jobs, a coherent social policy and move to boost economic growth.

But while governments regularly express concern at the EU's 10.8 percent rate of unemployment and sluggish economic growth, their room for manoeuvre is ringfenced by their efforts to slash budget deficits and debt in preparation for joining the bloc's single currency in 1999.
Feelings have been running high in Belgium since January when steelmaker Clabecq was declared bankrupt, putting 1,800 jobs at risk.
Tempers flared again in February when French carmaker Renault suddenly declared it would close its plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels in July with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
There have been sporadic, and occasionally violent, demonstrations by Belgian workers in Belgium and in France.
A major march for jobs through Brussels in March attracted up to 100,000 trades unionists and politicians from all over Europe. It passed without incident.
On Thursday in Charleroi the march will be accompanied by work stoppages at various local firms as well as on the regional railway.
